tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks (independent, README updated 2026-07-19) publishes the code (brainfuck/bf.lua vs brainfuck/bf_jit.lua, primes/primes.lua vs primes/primes_jit.lua, common/commands.mk runs `lua` and `luajit`), the interpreter builds in docker/Dockerfile (openresty/luajit2 v2.1-20260701 built with plain make, Debian lua package) and the CPU (Xeon E-2324G); the same-source kostya/jit-benchmarks run (nbody/test.lua, mandelbrot/test.lua, docker/lua and docker/luajit built from source with plain make, Ryzen 7 3800X) corroborates at A.

corrections.workload: kostya/benchmarks: Brainfuck interpreter (bench.b; mandel.b has LuaJIT only) and the primes test (Atkin sieve plus Trie prefix search). The two interpreters do NOT run the same script: LuaJIT runs bf_jit.lua and primes_jit.lua, which use LuaJIT's FFI (uint8_t[8192] tape, bool[] sieve) and the bit library, while Lua runs bf.lua and primes.lua with Lua tables and 5.3+ integer operators. Same-source corroboration: kostya/jit-benchmarks runs one test.lua per program under both `lua` and `luajit`.
corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks (different scripts per interpreter): bench.b Lua/luajit 5.686 s vs Lua 37.051 s (about 6.5x, derived from page data); primes Lua/luajit 0.309 s vs Lua 1.056 s (about 3.4x, derived from page data); mandel.b Lua/luajit 31.804 s with no plain-Lua row. Same-source kostya/jit-benchmarks (2023, LuaJIT 2.1.0-beta3 vs Lua 5.4.4): nbody 1.44 s vs 19.69 s (about 13.7x, derived from page data), mandelbrot 0.5 s vs 5.39 s (about 10.8x, derived from page data), spectralnorm 0.12 s vs 3.86 s; LuaJIT is slower on regexdna (9.99 s vs 8.94 s).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Interpreters run as `luajit file.lua` and `lua file.lua` (common/commands.mk). kostya/benchmarks: LuaJIT 2.1.1748495995 built with plain `make -j` from the openresty/luajit2 tag v2.1-20260701 (LuaJIT Makefile default flags) in docker/Dockerfile; Lua from the Debian package (README lists 5.4.7, Dockerfile installs lua5.5). kostya/jit-benchmarks: Lua 5.4.4 and openresty luajit2 2.1.0-beta3 both built from source with plain `make -j4` (docker/lua, docker/luajit).
corrections.hardware: kostya/benchmarks: Intel(R) Xeon(R) E-2324G, Docker (Debian forky/sid). kostya/jit-benchmarks: AMD Ryzen 7 3800X, Docker on Ubuntu 22.10.
corrections.caveats: In kostya/benchmarks the LuaJIT rows run different source files from the Lua rows (bf_jit.lua and primes_jit.lua use FFI C arrays and a fixed 8192-cell byte tape), so those ratios mix interpreter speed with FFI data structures; LuaJIT implements Lua 5.1 semantics (no integer subtype or native bitwise operators), which is why separate scripts exist. Same-source kostya/jit-benchmarks gives larger wins (nbody about 13.7x, mandelbrot about 10.8x) but is from 2023 with older versions, and LuaJIT loses regexdna there (9.99 s vs 8.94 s). The benchmarked binary is the openresty/luajit2 fork, not LuaJIT/LuaJIT itself. The kostya README says the baseline is Lua 5.4.7 but docker/Dockerfile installs Debian lua5.5 (both changed in the same 2026-07-19 commit), so the exact baseline version is uncertain. Single median timings on one machine per suite. The GitHub repository is a mirror of the official luajit.org git repository.

notes: Numbers match the kostya/benchmarks README rows and the jit-benchmarks tables; record wrongly said the same script ran under both interpreters (kostya uses FFI-based *_jit.lua files), corrected and added same-source jit-benchmarks numbers. Metadata checked: MIT, 5.8k stars, mirror (not archived), last commit 2026-09-08 on v2.1. Note the spec lists LuaJIT as a baseline of the 'jits' category; here it is filed under language-interpreters against Lua 5.x, which is a valid baseline.

tier_reason: First-party table in docs/benchmark.md: Octane scores for PrimJS vs QuickJS 6e2e68 on an Apple M1 Max with the PrimJS gn build args; the compiler is not named, the QuickJS build is not described and the repository has no Octane runner script, so it falls short of A and is first-party, hence C.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Octane (version 9) overall score 3735 vs 2904 for QuickJS 6e2e68 (about 1.29x, derived from page data; the README rounds it to about 28%). Per test: RayTrace 2751 vs 1273, EarleyBoyer 4270 vs 2284, NavierStokes 4166 vs 2640, PdfJS 6642 vs 4236, Crypto 1844 vs 1349, Richards 1247 vs 1163, Mandreel 1372 vs 1350; CodeLoad (16992 vs 18137) and MandreelLatency (9587 vs 9680) are lower.
corrections.caveats: First-party benchmark on one machine (Apple M1 Max, macOS) and one deprecated suite (Octane); compiler not named, QuickJS baseline build flags not given, no runner script in the repository. The speedups come from the template interpreter (embedded.S), snapshot, compatible memory management and tracing GC, which the README says are enabled by default only on arm64 targets with pre-generated embedded.S (Android, iOS, macOS) and stay disabled on Linux and non-arm64 targets, so the gain is not shown for x86-64 or Linux. Baseline is QuickJS, not V8 (the language-interpreters JS baseline); no memory or startup comparison. Built on QuickJS (MIT); the repository also carries MIT and BSD-3-Clause third-party code alongside Apache-2.0.

notes: Numbers match docs/benchmark.md exactly; downgraded A to C because it is first-party with no compiler, no baseline build description and no runner script. Metadata checked: Apache-2.0, 1.1k stars, not a GitHub fork but built on QuickJS, last commit 2026-09-29 on develop. QuickJS is a listed baseline of the embedded-scripting category, which may be a better home for this entry.

tier_reason: kostya/benchmarks runs the same Python files under both interpreters (brainfuck/bf3.py, matmul/matmul.py, primes/primes.py, json/test.py, base64/test.py via PYPY3_RUN and PYTHON3_RUN in common/commands.mk), with the PyPy 7.3.23 release tarball and Debian CPython in docker/Dockerfile and the Xeon E-2324G CPU stated; attractivechaos/plb2 independently confirms on an Apple M1 with public code and versions.

corrections.claimed_speedup: kostya/benchmarks: bench.b 9.398 s vs CPython 61.009 s (about 6.5x, derived from page data); matmul 3.263 s vs 136.267 s (about 42x, derived from page data); primes 0.617 s vs 1.725 s (about 2.8x, derived from page data); JSON 0.606 s vs 0.936 s (about 1.5x, derived from page data). base64 is slower: 3.534 s vs 3.099 s. plb2 (Apple M1, PyPy 7.3.14 vs CPython 3.11.7): nqueen 6.91 s vs 159.97 s, matmul 4.89 s vs 117.81 s, sudoku 8.82 s vs 52.88 s, bedcov 6.27 s vs 42.84 s.
corrections.stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; the GitHub repository has been PyPy's canonical repository and issue tracker since the December 2023 move from Heptapod
corrections.caveats: PyPy is slower than CPython on the kostya base64 test (3.534 s vs 3.099 s), so the win is workload dependent. PyPy uses more memory: base RSS about 60 MiB vs about 11 MiB for CPython in the kostya tables (JSON: 280.66 + 125.44 MiB vs 121.30 + 325.88 MiB). PyPy 7.3.23 implements Python 3.11 while the CPython baseline is 3.14.6. Whether the Debian CPython build has its experimental JIT enabled was not checked. Ratios are derived from medians on one machine per suite. Core is MIT; the bundled stdlib in lib-python is under the PSF license.

notes: All kostya and plb2 numbers match their rows; same source files run under both interpreters. Corrected the stale claim that GitHub is a mirror of Heptapod (PyPy moved its canonical repo to GitHub in December 2023; snippet from the pypy.org announcement plus GitHub PR merges in the commit log). Metadata checked: MIT (lib-python PSF), 1.8k stars, last commit 2026-10-05; the spec lists PyPy as a baseline of the 'jits' category, here it is filed under language-interpreters against CPython.
